entries.name: CHAIN Act
entries.content: CHAIN, short for Cooperative Human Assignment for Individual Needs, is a government program that allows individuals to voluntarily enter indentured servitude to pay off their debts. Under CHAIN, individuals are designated as "temporary property" for a fixed period, typically 3-6 months, and are assigned to government contractors or private trainers—often in labor-intensive industries, corporate research projects, or private domestic service—in exchange for total debt clearance. CHAIN is also sometimes used as a form of community service, though this is rarer due to prisons taking care of menial indentured labor instead. Their lobbying is rather fierce, ensuring they maintain their monopoly on this lucrative labor pool. Economists have praised CHAIN as an innovative approach to solving the nation's debt crisis

entries.name: BOND Collar
entries.content: The BOND Collar (Biometric Orthogonal Navigational Device) is a high-tech restraint and tracking device used primarily on CHAIN slaves. It can deliver mild to moderate electric shocks, act as a leash point, and is integrated with biometric monitors, GPS, and short-range communication devices. BOND collars are virtually impossible to remove without the proper key. It is legally required for those under the CHAIN act to wear them during their service.

entries.name: Slave Barcode
entries.content: Barcodes are another standard means of identifying CHAIN slaves. Applied as a tattoo or stamp on the inner wrist or other visible areas, these barcodes link to a database that contains all relevant information about the slave, including their name, CHAIN ID, contract terms, and authorized handlers. They are considered both a backup form of ID, and an added humiliation feature, marking the slave as mere property in the eyes of the law. Unlike BOND collars, barcodes are not legally required; a master can remove the barcode if they wish to. The tattoo itself is added via an ink stamper, with the ink formulation designed to rapidly disappear after exactly 3 or 6 months, depending on the sentencing.
